entries.subject: The mind is not a camera
entries.excerpt: In a 1998 field experiment, a person asking for directions was replaced while a door passed between the speakers. About half of pedestrians in the first experiment noticed. That is not a universal eyewitness-error rate. This week, learn to separate what an archival photograph actually shows from what we infer. Read The Missing Caption.
entries.word_budget_note: Curiosity-led editorial. WordPress should append its own read-more link to the full post.

entries.subject: Before hypnosis had a name
entries.excerpt: In May 1784, Puységur described a young farmworker who reportedly slept, spoke and later remembered nothing. His account records testimony, not proof of Mesmer's magnetic fluid. We examine the surviving record, later interpretations and what France's royal commission did—and did not—study. Read Puységur's Animal Magnetism Files.
entries.word_budget_note: Source-led history. Do not imply the historical reports establish a magnetic fluid.

entries.subject: Seventeen seconds. A much longer explanation.
entries.excerpt: The Apollo 204 Review Board logged 17.1 seconds between the first recorded crew report of fire and the end of the last transmission. That interval does not reveal the precise ignition instant or source. The record instead exposes interacting hazards: oxygen, combustible materials and an inward-opening hatch. Read The Hatch Opened Inward.
entries.word_budget_note: Check NASA's original timeline at production. No invented certainty about ignition source.

entries.subject: What did seven days of attention reveal?
entries.excerpt: Seven days of attention notes can show when a routine worked; they cannot prove improved concentration. A 2002 study of paper diaries monitored with sensors shows why recording time matters. Use our four-line evidence log, leave missing entries missing, and open the free Seven Day Focus Fieldbook to continue. No audio purchase required.
